class_id: a claim-time filter on a counter that only ever increases is a TERMINAL state that no code can reverse, while the row's own state field still reads transient
feature: any work-queue table whose rows are selected by a predicate over a monotonically-increasing attempt/retry/failure counter, where the counter is never reset and the row's `state` column is deliberately left non-terminal
symptom: a queue bounds churn by refusing to hand out rows past an attempt cap — `WHERE state = '<retryable>' AND attempts < MAX` — and documents this as a claim-time FILTER, explicitly not a state transition, so that the row is not retired. The intent is that the condition is TRANSIENT and the row becomes workable again once the blocker is removed. But if nothing ever RESETS the counter, the filter is terminal in every way that matters: the row can never be selected again, by any code path, forever. The state column still says retryable, so no completion report counts it as done; the filter excludes it, so no pending report counts it as work. The population falls into the gap between the two and is invisible to both. The failure is worst precisely where the design is most careful: a row blocked by a DEPLOYMENT gap (a missing adapter, an unconfigured credential, a feature flag off) burns its attempt budget on a condition that has nothing to do with the row, and when the gap is closed the row does not come back. Universal shape: transience must be enforced at the layer the SELECT reads. A transient `state` plus a permanent counter, where the query reads the counter, is a terminal state with a transient label. Any 'registering X must be enough to make this askable again' guarantee is false unless closing the gap also clears whatever the claim predicate reads.
first_seen: 2026-09-22 -- `ipo_field_plan` in IPODhan, measured read-only on `ipodhan_staging` through the sanctioned tunnel. 154 rows carry `cause LIKE '%NO_FETCHER_REGISTERED%'` (reason_code SOURCE_UNREACHABLE), every one source = NSE, across 17 distinct IPOs; 144 of the 154 sit at exactly `attempts = 5`, which is `FIELD_PLAN_RECLAIM_MAX_ATTEMPTS` (ipo-field-plan-repository.ts:118). All 154 are past due (`due_now` 154 of 154 at utc_now 2026-09-22 12:40:00) and none has been attempted since 2026-09-20 21:16:01 UTC. The claim query filters `state = 'CHECK_FAILED' AND attempts < FIELD_PLAN_RECLAIM_MAX_ATTEMPTS` at :809 and :815, and its own comment states it is 'a claim-time FILTER, never a state transition -- the row is not moved to EXHAUSTED'. Every write to `attempts` in that repository was grepped: there is exactly ONE, the increment at :967, and the plan-regeneration upsert's `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE` set-list (:453-461) updates ranks, manifest_version, policy_origin and updated_at but touches neither `attempts` nor `state`, so not even a manifest-version bump recovers them. The timeline is the finding: last attempt 2026-09-20 21:16 UTC, and PR #867 registered the NSE fetcher at 2026-09-21 00:22 IST -- the rows stopped being askable hours BEFORE the thing that would have answered them arrived. `field-plan-walk.ts:700-711` had named this exact risk in advance: 'TRANSIENT: a missing adapter is a deployment/config state ... Registering the adapter must be enough to make the field askable again -- retiring it terminally would mean a config gap silently outlived its own fix.' The guard was placed on the STATE (sawTransientFailure keeps the row out of EXHAUSTED) while the SELECT reads the COUNTER, so the config gap outlived its own fix exactly as warned. Affected fields are live reader-facing ones: listing_performance.current_price_nse (17), ipo_demand_graph.{cumulative_quantity,exchange,is_cut_off,price_point} (7 each), subscriptions.{b_nii,s_nii,employee,shares_offered,total_shares_bid} (7 each), ipo_details.* (6 each), ipos.lot_size (6), ipos.face_value (2). Filed as #884
fix_prs: not yet fixed -- filed as #884 with the measurement. Three parts, in order: (1) a transient failure must not consume a permanent budget -- either do not increment `attempts` when the only failure was NO_FETCHER_REGISTERED (the walk already distinguishes this; it sets `sawTransientFailure`), or count transient and real failures in separate columns so the claim predicate reads only the real ones; (2) the 144 existing rows cannot recover on their own and need a productized, re-runnable repair tool (dry-run default, prod guard), never hand SQL; (3) the detection below. Note for whoever builds it: #759 proposed the OPPOSITE fix for the same condition -- a terminal `NO_FETCHER` enum member -- and that would deepen this defect rather than fix it, for the reason field-plan-walk.ts's own comment gives
detection_check: none, and its absence is why this survived two days on an actively-watched staging box. The gap is structural, not an oversight: `pull_exhaust` reads rows in state EXHAUSTED, and these rows are deliberately NOT in EXHAUSTED; nothing at all reads 'non-terminal state AND past the claim predicate'. The check to build is exactly that population -- rows whose `state` is retryable but which the claim query can never select again -- reported by reason_code and by source, diffed NEW/GONE/SAME nightly. It generalises to any queue with a monotonic cap: the query is 'rows the SELECT excludes that the STATE says are still pending', and a healthy queue holds zero of them. A check that counts only terminal-state rows is structurally blind to this class, the same way a population-by-JOIN can never detect a missing member of that population
